To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the prevalence of hypertension is high in the United States and worldwide, (2) it is a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and disability, and (3) it is largely preventable.

(a) a risk score for risk factor (RSRF) approach is useful in identifying individuals at high risk for hypertension; (b) a RSRF can be used to identify the most important risk factors for hypertension and to determine which risk factors to target; and (c) the RSRF approach can be used to estimate the impact of a given level of reduction in risk factors on the prevalence of hypertension.

(1) the prevalence of hypertension is higher in black than in white men and women; (2) the prevalence of prehypertension is also higher in black than white men and women, and the prevalence of hypertension and prehypertension in blacks is increasing; and (3) the prevalence of suboptimal BP is increasing in both men and women, but more rapidly in women than in men.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epidemiology of chronic disease and its prevention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the most important causes of hypertension are genetic and environmental, but that these factors are not independent and that the relative contribution of each depends on the population under study, and that the most effective means of prevention is to reduce the environmental causes.

the risk factors for hypertension include obesity, high dietary sodium, low potassium, low fruit and vegetable intake, low calcium intake, high alcohol intake, high stress, high socioeconomic stress, and low education.
hypertension is the result of a complex interplay between genetic factors, environmental factors, and chance events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of hypertension in the United States has decreased over the last 20 years.
the prevalence of hypertension in the US is 29%, with 17% having prehypertension and 12% having hypertension.

the risk of cardiovascular events is directly related to the level of blood pressure and that the risk of death is related to the duration of the high blood pressure, the higher the blood pressure the shorter the duration of the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the population-attributable risk of hypertension is very high.
there is a strong rationale for using a risk score for risk factor to guide prevention efforts.
there are many different risk factors that contribute to hypertension.
